topic: Space-Filling Curves: Folding a Line into a Square
target_audience: University students (Computer Science, Mathematics, or Physics)

sections.title: The Dimensionality Paradox
lecture_lines: Can a one-dimensional line cover a two-dimensional square?
Intuitively, a line is thin and lacks area.
However, a dense map can fill every point.
Imagine a snail leaving a trail across the floor.
Can its path touch every single point in space?
animations: Create a simple horizontal line in the center (Color: #FFFFFF).
Create a square outline (Color: #FFFF00) and scale the line to fit inside.
The line starts to fold into a basic U-shape (Level 1).
A small green circle (Color: #00FF00) representing the 'Quantum Snail' appears at the start.
The line rapidly increases in complexity (Level 5) until the square appears filled with green.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Iteration and Limits
lecture_lines: Space-filling curves result from repeating a simple process.
We divide a square into four smaller quadrants.
Infinite repetition creates a dense, nested grid structure.
animations: Draw a large square (Color: #FFFFFF).
Divide the square into a 2x2 grid using grey lines (Color: #808080).
Subdivide each of the 4 quadrants into another 2x2 grid (Color: #808080).

sections.title: The Hilbert Curve Construction
lecture_lines: The Hilbert curve begins with a basic U-shape.
We rotate and flip this shape in each quadrant.
Connecting segments join these pieces into a single line.
Increasing iterations fills the square with more detail.
Eventually, the line becomes a solid block of color.
animations: Display Level 1 Hilbert Curve (U-shape) in cyan (Color: #00FFFF).
Morph Level 1 into Level 2 (four U-shapes, rotated and connected).
Morph Level 2 into Level 3 (16 U-shapes, connected).
Morph Level 3 into Level 4 (64 U-shapes, connected).
Flash the entire curve to emphasize its continuous nature (Color: #FFFFFF).

sections.title: Mathematical Mapping: [0, 1] → [0, 1]²
lecture_lines: We map intervals on a line to 2D coordinates.
The function is continuous, never lifting the pen.
It is surjective, hitting every point in the square.
animations: Display a 1D line segment [0, 1] (Color: #FFFFFF) at the bottom.
Display a 2D square [0, 1]^2 (Color: #FFFFFF) above it.
A red dot (Color: #FF0000) moves along the 1D segment from 0 to 1.
A second red dot (Color: #FF0000) moves along a high-level Hilbert curve in the square.
Label the 1D point 't' and the 2D point 'f(t)' (Color: #FFFFFF).

sections.title: Key Property: Locality Preservation
lecture_lines: Nearby points on the line remain nearby in space.
This locality preservation is useful for data clustering.
The curve cleans one region before moving to another.
animations: Highlight a segment on the 1D line (Color: #FFA500).
Highlight the corresponding 'local' region in the 2D Hilbert curve (Color: #FFA500).
Pulse the highlighted regions to show they stay clustered together.

sections.title: Modern Applications: From Maps to Data
lecture_lines: These curves flatten 2D images into 1D data.
Preserving neighbor pixels significantly improves image compression.
Databases use this for efficient range queries.
Google Maps indexes locations using space-filling curves.
Abstract math solves real-world high-dimensional data problems.
animations: Show a 4x4 grid of colored blocks.
Draw a Hilbert curve path through all blocks (Color: #FFFFFF).
Flatten the grid into a 1D row of blocks according to the path order.
